Using nn.functional.interpolate is very slow when using mixed precision training. This seems to have already been an issue in the past (#12409) and should be fixed, but I am still seeing a performance regression of up to 5x (yes, that is 5x the runtime of fp32) depending on the network an GPU.
To demonstrate the issue I have created a small script that reproduces it. I am mostly interested in 3D images which is why that example uses 3D convs, but the same issue appears also with 2D inputs (see below, I will add a separate section for that).
What my script does is the following:
It builds a very simple convolutional encoder network (VGG style) that downsamples the input 1x64x64x64 to 512x4x4x4. It then blows up the small representation back to 512x64x64x64 using interpolate. The loss is then simple the MSE between input and upsampled output.
This workflow does not represent a useful application, it is just there to put some load on the GPU and isolate the issue.
I run 100 iterations with this setup in three settings

regular fp32
regular AMP
AMP but with a hack: the encoding (512x4x4x4 tensor) is cast to float, then upsampled and then cast to half.

Expected behavior:
2. should be much faster than 1. due to tensor core acceleration of the convolutions, 3. should be slower than 2. due to additional overhead (casting)
Actual behavior:
2. is slower than 1.. 3. is faster than 2.
Environment:
I am using pytorch 1.7.0 compiled with cuDNN 8.0.5.39. OS is Ubuntu 18.04 (RTX 3090) and centOS (RTX 2080ti, V100).
I am also showing results for 1.7.1 with cuDNN 7.6.5 (installed with pip today) to demonstrate that is not related to my build.
Details and standalone script
from time import time

from torch import nn
import torch
from torch.cuda.amp import GradScaler, autocast
from torch.nn import functional
from torch.optim import SGD


class Network(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cast_for_upsample=False):
        super().__init__()
        self.cast_for_upsample = cast_for_upsample

        self.layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv3d(1, 32, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),
            nn.Conv3d(32, 32, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),

            nn.Conv3d(32, 64, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),
            nn.Conv3d(64, 64, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),

            nn.Conv3d(64, 128, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),
            nn.Conv3d(128, 128, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),

            nn.Conv3d(128, 256, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),
            nn.Conv3d(256, 256, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),

            nn.Conv3d(256, 512, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),
            nn.Conv3d(512, 512, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, False),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        down = self.layers(x)
        if self.cast_for_upsample:
            up = nn.functional.interpolate(down.float(), x.shape[2:], None, 'trilinear').half()
        else:
            up = nn.functional.interpolate(down, x.shape[2:], None, 'trilinear')
        return up


if __name__ == "__main__":
    inp = torch.rand((2, 1, 64, 64, 64)).cuda()

    net = Network(cast_for_upsample=False).cuda()
    optimizer = SGD(net.parameters(), 0.001)

    torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    # warmup
    for _ in range(10):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        out = net(inp)
        l = torch.square(inp - out).mean() # just the MSE between input and output as a dummy loss function
        l.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    # fp32 measurement
    st = time()
    for _ in range(100):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        out = net(inp)
        l = torch.square(inp - out).mean() # just the MSE between input and output as a dummy loss function
        l.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    print('fp32:', time() - st)

    ####################################################
    # now AMP
    net = Network(cast_for_upsample=False).cuda()
    optimizer = SGD(net.parameters(), 0.001)
    scaler = GradScaler()

    torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    # warmup
    for _ in range(10):
        optimizer.zero_grad()

        with autocast():
            out = net(inp)
            l = torch.square(inp - out).mean()  # just the MSE between input and output as a dummy loss function

        scaler.scale(l).backward()
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()

    # amp measurement
    st = time()
    for _ in range(100):
        optimizer.zero_grad()

        with autocast():
            out = net(inp)
            l = torch.square(inp - out).mean()  # just the MSE between input and output as a dummy loss function

        scaler.scale(l).backward()
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()
    print('amp:', time() - st)

    ####################################################
    # now AMP with hacking interpolate so that is runs in fp32
    net = Network(cast_for_upsample=True).cuda()
    optimizer = SGD(net.parameters(), 0.001)
    scaler = GradScaler()

    torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    # warmup
    for _ in range(10):
        optimizer.zero_grad()

        with autocast():
            out = net(inp)
            l = torch.square(inp - out).mean()  # just the MSE between input and output as a dummy loss function

        scaler.scale(l).backward()
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()

    # amp measurement
    st = time()
    for _ in range(100):
        optimizer.zero_grad()

        with autocast():
            out = net(inp)
            l = torch.square(inp - out).mean()  # just the MSE between input and output as a dummy loss function

        scaler.scale(l).backward()
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()
    print('amp cast to float:', time() - st)

🚀 Feature
Request support for exporting the new nn.PixelUnshuffle / F.pixel_unshuffle operation to ONNX using torch.onnx.export.
Motivation
The "PixelUnshuffle" operation, also known as "SpaceToDepth", was recently added to torch with this feature request. This operation is the inverse of the "PixelShuffle" / "DepthToSpace" operation, and both operations have been supported by ONNX since at least opset 9. However, torch only supports exporting PixelShuffle, and not PixelUnshuffle, to ONNX. This precludes users' ability to deploy models trained in torch that include PixelUnshuffle layers to ONNX (and other) runtimes. Such models include convolutional U-nets, autoencoders, super-resolution models, and many others that require efficient lossless spatial re-sampling.
Example:
import torch

layer = torch.nn.PixelUnshuffle(2)

x = torch.rand(1, 1, 2, 2)

assert (layer(x) == x.view(1, 4, 1, 1)).all().item()  # passes

for opset_version in range(9, 14):
    try:
        torch.onnx.export(layer, x, "./pixel_unshuffle.onnx", opset_version=opset_version)
    except RuntimeError as err:
        print(err)
Prints for every version:
Exporting the operator pixel_unshuffle to ONNX opset version <version> is not supported. Please open a bug to request ONNX export support for the missing operator.

Pitch
In order to achieve parity with PixelShuffle, and in order to support deploying the many vision models that require it, I request that torch developers please add support for exporting the PixelUnshuffle operation to ONNX.
Alternatives
This feature is in fact present in tensorflow and tf2onnx, so I am currently using that framework for my particular use case. This induces hassle and stress among my group, as we would prefer to stick to a single framework.
Additional context
I was advised to file a feature request by @mruberry here.

🐛 Bug
Batched gradient computation warns when a batching rule is not implemented. However, warnings during backward execution may not be turned into Python warnings, leading to console spam (#50209)
To Reproduce
import torch
from torch._vmap_internals import vmap
import warnings
warnings.simplefilter('ignore')

device = 'cuda:0'
x = torch.randn(4, requires_grad=True, device=device)
indices = torch.tensor([0, 1], device=device)
y = x.gather(0, indices)

def vjp(v):
    return torch.autograd.grad(y, x, v, retain_graph=True)

vs = torch.randn(2, *y.shape, device=device)
vmap(vjp)(vs)
vmap(vjp)(vs)
vmap(vjp)(vs)

# This script has the following output, despite the warnings filter
# [W BatchedFallback.cpp:63] Warning: Batching rule not implemented for aten::gather_backward falling back to slow (for loop and stack) implementation (function batchedTensorForLoopFallback)
# [W BatchedFallback.cpp:63] Warning: Batching rule not implemented for aten::gather_backward falling back to slow (for loop and stack) implementation (function batchedTensorForLoopFallback)
# [W BatchedFallback.cpp:63] Warning: Batching rule not implemented for aten::gather_backward falling back to slow (for loop and stack) implementation (function batchedTensorForLoopFallback)
Challenges
I don't think we are going to fix #50209 anytime soon. Furthermore, using TORCH_WARN_ONCE doesn't solve the problem because all operators that go through the fallback use the same exact vmap warning generation code; TORCH_WARN_ONCE would cause the warning to appear only at the first operator that raises the warning.
Any solution must take into account that autograd is multi-threaded.
Potential solutions
Here are a few different proposals for this, categorized into "short-term" and "long-term". I am not suggesting that we do something in the short-term bucket first.
"Short-term"

Implement a VMAP_WARN_ONCE that allocates a hash map on a heap. If an operator is not in the hash map, then we print a warning and add it to the map. If it is in the map, then we do not print the warning. (Is adding elements to std::unordered_map thread safe?)
By default, disable the vmap fallback warning. Add a private _ShowVmapWarnings context manager that enables the vmap fallback warning. We already have a mechanism to handle propagating thread-local state through autograd threads

"long term"

These functions are necessary for proper and easy use of FFT, which has been recently added to PyTorch #42175.

On Ubuntu 20.04 x86_64, by default, apt-get installs LAPACK in its corresponding subdirectory in /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/.
